content: In mathematics, the concept of a measure extends the ideas of length, area, and volume, but it is not limited to physical dimensions. Informally, a measure assigns a consistent size to certain subsets of a given base set. Depending on the context, this size can represent physical dimensions, the quantity of something within the subset, or the probability of a random process producing an outcome within the subset. Measures are primarily used to define generalized notions of integration over domains with more complex structures than simple intervals on the real line. These integrals are widely applied in probability theory and mathematical analysis. It is not always feasible or necessary to assign a size to every subset of the base set, so measures are not required to do so. Instead, certain consistency conditions dictate which subsets can be assigned sizes, and these conditions are formalized through the concept of a σ-algebra. Measure theory, a branch of real analysis, studies σ-algebras, measures, measurable functions, and integrals. A measure space is defined as a triple (X, Σ, μ), where X is the base set, Σ is the σ-algebra of measurable subsets, and μ is the measure. If μ(X) = 1, the measure space is called a probability space, and μ is referred to as a probability measure. For measure spaces that are also topological spaces, compatibility conditions can be imposed between the measure and the topology. Most measures encountered in analysis and probability theory are Radon measures, which can also be defined in terms of linear functionals on the space of continuous functions with compact support. This approach is used by authors such as Bourbaki. Several properties of measures can be derived from the definition of countable additivity. For example, measures are monotonic: if one measurable set is a subset of another, the measure of the smaller set is less than or equal to the measure of the larger set. Additionally, the intersection of a decreasing sequence of measurable sets is measurable, provided at least one of the sets has finite measure. Without this assumption, the property may fail, as demonstrated by examples involving sets with infinite measure. A measure space is finite if the measure of the entire space is a finite real number. It is σ-finite if the space can be decomposed into a countable union of measurable sets with finite measure. For instance, the real numbers with the standard Lebesgue measure are σ-finite but not finite. In contrast, the real numbers with the counting measure are not σ-finite because covering the entire real line would require uncountably many finite sets. A measurable set is called a null set if its measure is zero. A subset of a null set is termed a negligible set. While negligible sets are not necessarily measurable, any measurable negligible set is automatically a null set. A measure is complete if every negligible set is measurable. Measures can be extended to complete measures by considering subsets that differ from measurable sets by a null set. Examples of important measures include the following: The counting measure, which assigns to a set the number of its elements. The Lebesgue measure, the unique complete translation-invariant measure on a σ-algebra containing the intervals in ℝ, with μ([0,1]) = 1. The circular angle measure, which is invariant under rotation. The Haar measure, a generalization of the Lebesgue measure for locally compact topological groups, with a similar uniqueness property. The Hausdorff measure, which refines the Lebesgue measure to apply to certain fractal sets. Probability measures, which assign a total measure of 1 to the entire space, as seen in probability spaces. The Dirac measure, which assigns a measure of 1 to any set containing a specific point and 0 otherwise. Other measures include the Borel measure, Jordan measure, ergodic measure, Euler measure, Gauss measure, Baire measure, and Radon measure. Not all subsets of Euclidean space are Lebesgue measurable. Examples of non-measurable sets include the Vitali set and those arising from the Hausdorff paradox and the Banach–Tarski paradox. Generalizations of measures allow for values beyond the non-negative reals or infinity. For example, a signed measure takes values in the real numbers, while a complex measure takes values in the complex numbers. Measures taking values in Banach spaces have also been extensively studied. A measure that takes values in the set of self-adjoint projections on a Hilbert space is called a projection-valued measure and is used in functional analysis, particularly in the spectral theorem. To distinguish standard measures from these generalizations, the term positive measure is used for measures with non-negative values. Another generalization is the finitely additive measure, which requires only finite additivity instead of countable additivity. Historically, this definition was used first but proved less useful. Finitely additive measures are connected to concepts such as Banach limits, the dual of L∞, and the Stone–Čech compactification, all of which are related to the axiom of choice. Homogeneous measures of various degrees are also studied. For example: A measure homogeneous of degree ( n ) corresponds to the ordinary ( n )-dimensional volume. A measure homogeneous of degree ( n-1 ) corresponds to surface volume. A measure homogeneous of degree 1 is known as the mean width, though the term is somewhat misleading. A measure homogeneous of degree 0 corresponds to the Euler characteristic.
